author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow: it lays rollback out as one straight sequence (freeze, drain, reconcile, reprocess, resume) in a single diagram, and each step says what starts it and where its state is kept. A asks the reader to work out claim races between the two engines running at once, repeats its rollback sub-diagram twice, and includes a "mark paid" step that writes nothing.

author: haiku
reason: A gives one linear rollback path (freeze, drain, reconcile, optional reprocess, resume) and says for each step what starts it and where its state lives; B duplicates the rollback in two near-identical sub-machines, includes a step that writes nothing ("mark paid"), and leaves the reader to work out how the claims settle races after the flip.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to follow: its rollback steps have names that say what they do (pause_charging, drain_in_flight, reconcile_ledger, handover), it names what starts each step (a charge monitor writes the rollback record, which starts the runner), and it explains how gates reset with one epoch counter, while A takes longer to parse because it lists the shadow rollback as a numbered step, adds the pin machinery, and keeps a reprocess step whose purpose it questions itself.

author: sonnet
reason: A sets out each rollback step with a clear trigger, says exactly where state lives (flag, rollback record, change history, epoch-tagged counters), and keeps every step coherent; B adds extra ideas (event pinning, the affected window, a no-charge exception for shadow rollbacks), and its own open questions say its reprocess step may be unnecessary, which makes it harder to follow.

author: haiku
reason: B gives the same core flow through a short summary, a cleaner diagram, nine plainly triggered steps and a failure table tied to those steps, so a newcomer understands it faster; A covers more ground, but its 30-term glossary, crowded 40-node diagram with note arrows, and tangled retry and recovery prose slow that understanding more than B's small slip of storing the event id twice.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is easier to follow: one tight summary, a flowchart that matches its nine short steps, and gaps that are named plainly as open; Document B covers more ground but adds extra machinery (hold-expired flag, saved payment outcome, background worker, recovery job) and has conflicting charge-retry rules ("Order does not resend" against recovery resending the charge), which slows a newcomer down and invites misreading.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to follow: it uses events throughout, and each numbered step names its service and the event that starts it, in a clear happy-path status sequence. A mixes HTTP and events and adds patch-like branches, such as the two CHECKOUT_FAILED variants, refunds for orders that already failed, and SUCCEEDED overwriting DECLINED, which make its flowchart and steps harder to trace.

author: sonnet
reason: A uses one mechanism throughout: a single HTTP call, then events delivered through an outbox, with acknowledgement and inbox rules defined up front, and every diagram arrow names the event that starts the next step; B mixes HTTP replies, events and retries, breaks its own solid/dotted arrow legend (for example the dotted 'any line short' arrow), and adds special cases such as overwriting DECLINED with SUCCEEDED and the separate CHECKOUT_FAILED refund paths, which make the flow harder to follow correctly.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow because each row's route is fixed when it is inserted, and the flow then runs Enqueue, Publish, Accept, Send, Report, Record and Reconcile, each saying what starts it, where its state lives and what happens on failure; A makes the reader hold more moving parts at once: an owner column that can go back to NULL after a crash, a flag read at claim time, a three-part relay, carried-over attempt counts and a 20-hour guard.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is easier to follow because of its simple model: each row's route is set once at insert and never changes. Its numbered flow gives each step one trigger, the state it touches and its failure behaviour. Document B relies on owner states that are claimed at an unpredictable time, a 20-hour guard, page intents and a long passage about event ordering, and it contradicts itself on cross-database reconciliation, so the reader has to do much more work to build a correct picture.

author: sonnet
reason: Document B is easier to follow: its "How it runs" section walks one notification through eight numbered steps (Record, Dispatch, Receive, Send, Page, Publish outcome, Apply outcome, Reconcile), and each step says what triggers it, what state changes and what happens on failure, with terms like lease, due and outbox defined first, whereas Document A describes each component separately and leaves the reader to piece the end-to-end flow together.

author: sonnet
reason: A walks through the flow in order (record, dispatch, receive, send, page, publish outcome, apply outcome, reconcile), and each step says what starts it, where its state lives and what happens on failure; B groups the same mechanics by component and reuses `pending` as a service status, so the reader has to piece the sequence together.

author: haiku
reason: A is clearer because each flow opens with what starts it, then gives numbered steps that say where state lives and what happens on failure, and a failure table brings those cases together; B spreads the mechanism and its error handling across a dense Decisions table and a diagram that leaves out the failure paths.

author: haiku
reason: B walks through each flow as numbered steps that say what starts them, puts a failure branch on every step, and ends with a table of what state is left behind after each failure; A spreads the same behaviour across a large decisions table, a diagram that leaves out login storage errors, and a separate rules section.
